title: The Programmable Data Center — Evan Conrad, SF Compute
subtitle: From GPU trading to physical settlement, independent markets, and programmable compute
intro: This was recorded on the sidelines of the new Compute Trading track at AIE NYC . Catch us next at AIE CODE , our last flagship for the top agentic engineers in the world.
In the early days of cloud, former guest Martin Casado made something so disruptive that Cisco was threatened enough to pay $600m for it, and VMware outbid for $1.3B:

That concept was software-defined networking , which virtualized the routing network by separating the control plane from the data plane. That revolution is now coming for GPUs - where previously running your own supercompute cluster required $50-100m upfront to get commitments and do the entire stack from hardware to firmware to kernels, SF Compute is now enabling you to not only buy or sell GPU hours now and in the future, but also to programmatically control everything from your network to memory.

We last spoke with Evan about commoditizing compute . At AI Engineer New York, we went deeper: what does it take to physically deliver a GPU contract, and what has to be true before a market in compute can become liquid?

Evan describes SF Compute’s expansion with a hotel analogy. A customer wants a room, then asks for cleaning, room service, and security. Eventually you discover that delivering the room means operating the hotel. SF Compute began by trying to sublease a cluster; the company has since built much of the operating capacity of a cloud to deliver the compute traded on its market.

That work is physical settlement: the buyer gets usable compute, rather than simply a cash payment against an index. It brings the physical constraints of a cluster into the market itself. Can a workload be interrupted? How quickly can it recover from storage? Which GPU generation, networking and software configuration does it need? Those details affect both the contract and the price.

Rather than waiting for every GPU cluster to become interchangeable, SF Compute matches orders with different constraints. Evan argues that this makes trading possible while the technology changes, at the cost of spreading liquidity across more variants. We also discuss spot and forward pricing, batch versus live inference, and why an index can become disconnected from the cost of actually buying compute.

Independence is central to Evan’s case for a market operator. He argues that companies with large hardware or inference businesses have incentives that make it harder to run a neutral exchange. We also get into the unglamorous engineering: visiting sites, designing clusters, running the backplane, and making infrastructure programmable. Near the end, he describes the ability to subdivide InfiniBand fabric on the fly as one example.
Guest: Evan Conrad, CEO of SF Compute .

summary.one_liner: 解析 SF Compute 如何藉由可程式化資料中心與實體交割機制，建立具彈性的獨立 GPU 交易市場。

topics.title: 軟體定義 GPU 與可程式化運算
topics.body: 過去建立超級運算叢集需要預付 5000 萬至 1 億美元，並自行處理從硬體、韌體到核心的整套架構。SF Compute 借鑑軟體定義網路（SDN）將控制層與資料層分離的概念，讓使用者不僅能買賣現在與未來的 GPU 時數，還能以程式化方式全面控制網路與記憶體。

topics.title: 飯店隱喻與實體交割雲端營運
topics.body: Evan 以經營飯店比喻公司的擴展歷程：客戶最初只要房間，隨後需要清潔、客房服務與保全，最後發現交付房間等同於營運整座飯店。SF Compute 最初嘗試轉租叢集，如今已建立起完整的雲端營運能力，確保買方能獲得真正可用的算力，而非單純對照指數的現金結算。

topics.title: 物理限制對合約與定價的影響
topics.body: 實體交割會將叢集的物理限制帶入市場機制中。工作負載能否被中斷、從儲存復原的速度，以及所需的 GPU 世代、網路與軟體配置，都會直接影響合約內容與價格。SF Compute 透過媒合具備不同約束條件的訂單，在技術快速更迭的同時促成交易。

topics.title: 中立市場營運商的獨立性
topics.body: Evan 強調市場營運商保持獨立至關重要。本身擁有龐大硬體或推論業務的公司存在利益衝突，難以維持中立的交易平台。此外，缺乏實體交付機制的算力指數容易與實際採購成本脫節，獨立營運商才能客觀反映現貨與遠期定價。

topics.title: 底層基礎設施與動態分割網路
topics.body: 推動算力市場需要大量扎實且繁瑣的底層工程，包含實地場勘、叢集設計與背板維運。為了讓基礎設施完全可程式化，SF Compute 實現了即時動態細分 InfiniBand 網路架構（fabric）等能力，以因應不同規模的運算需求。

insights.title: 區分批次與即時推論以最佳化算力成本
insights.body: 在設計 Agent 工作流或大規模 RAG 嵌入管線時，應依據中斷容忍度將任務拆分為批次推論與即時推論，以便利用具彈性定價的現貨算力降低營運成本。

insights.title: 將硬體與網路物理限制納入架構評估
insights.body: 評估模型部署時，需考量狀態復原時間、儲存讀取速度與 InfiniBand 網路拓撲等底層約束，避免分散式系統在擴展時遭遇網路架構瓶頸。

insights.title: 提防抽象算力指標與實際交付成本脫鉤
insights.body: 規劃長期 AI 系統的基礎設施預算時，應關注具備實體交付保障的合約，而非僅參考名目運算指數，以確保硬體規格與延遲表現符合預期。

guests.name: Evan Conrad
guests.intro: SF Compute 執行長，致力於打造獨立的 GPU 算力交易市場，並推動資料中心基礎架構的可程式化與實體交割。

summary.one_liner: Analyzing how SF Compute builds a flexible, independent GPU marketplace through programmable data centers and physical delivery mechanisms.

topics.title: Software-Defined GPUs and Programmable Compute
topics.body: In the past, building a supercomputing cluster required an upfront investment of $50M to $100M and managing the entire stack—from hardware and firmware down to the kernel. Drawing on the concept of separating the control plane from the data plane in software-defined networking (SDN), SF Compute allows users not only to trade current and future GPU hours, but also to maintain full programmatic control over networking and memory.

topics.title: The Hotel Metaphor and Physical Delivery Cloud Operations
topics.body: Evan uses running a hotel as an analogy for the company's scaling journey: customers initially just want a room, then need housekeeping, room service, and security, until you realize that delivering a room is equivalent to operating the entire hotel. SF Compute started out attempting to sublease clusters, but has now built out full-fledged cloud operations capabilities, ensuring buyers receive truly usable compute rather than cash-settled contracts pegged to an index.

topics.title: The Impact of Physical Constraints on Contracts and Pricing
topics.body: Physical delivery brings the cluster's physical constraints into the market mechanism. Whether a workload is interruptible, how fast it can recover from storage, and the required GPU generation, networking, and software stack all directly dictate contract terms and pricing. By matching orders with differing constraints, SF Compute facilitates transactions even amidst rapid technological turnover.

topics.title: The Independence of a Neutral Marketplace Operator
topics.body: Evan emphasizes that it is critical for a marketplace operator to remain independent. Companies with substantial proprietary hardware or inference operations face conflicts of interest, making it difficult to sustain a neutral trading platform. Furthermore, compute indices lacking physical delivery mechanisms easily detach from actual procurement costs; only an independent operator can objectively reflect spot and forward pricing.

topics.title: Underlying Infrastructure and Dynamically Partitioned Fabrics
topics.body: Powering a compute marketplace demands extensive, rigorous low-level engineering, including site surveys, cluster design, and backplane maintenance. To make infrastructure fully programmable, SF Compute engineered capabilities such as real-time dynamic partitioning of the InfiniBand fabric to support compute demands of varying scales.

insights.title: Differentiating Batch vs. Real-Time Inference to Optimize Compute Costs
insights.body: When designing agentic workflows or large-scale RAG embedding pipelines, tasks should be partitioned into batch and real-time inference based on fault tolerance, enabling teams to leverage flexibly priced spot compute to drive down operational costs.

insights.title: Incorporating Hardware and Network Physical Constraints into Architecture Evaluation
insights.body: When evaluating model deployments, low-level constraints such as state recovery time, storage throughput, and InfiniBand network topology must be accounted for to prevent distributed systems from hitting fabric bottlenecks during scale-out.

insights.title: Beware of Abstract Compute Metrics Decoupled from Actual Delivery Costs
insights.body: When planning long-term AI infrastructure budgets, focus on contracts backed by physical delivery guarantees rather than nominal compute indices alone, ensuring hardware specifications and latency profiles meet expectations.
